findings.title: Google credential key is overwritten with a zod safeParse result object
findings.body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse()` returns a zod `safeParse` result (`{ success: true, data: {...} }`), not the parsed credential. The old code was `const key = googleCredentialSchema.parse(googleCredentials)`, which returned the keys themselves. Now `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })` persists `{"success":true,"data":{...}}` as the credential key. After the first access-token refresh, `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` in `googleAuth()` will fail and the user's Google Calendar integration is permanently broken until they reconnect. Either return `.data` from the helper or use `parseRefreshTokenResponse(...).data` here.

findings.title: minimumTokenResponseSchema is built from invalid computed keys and strips all other fields
findings.body: `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` do not produce dynamic key matchers: `ZodString.toString()` yields the string "[object Object]", so both computed properties collapse into a single literal key `"[object Object]"` (the second definition overwriting the first). The schema therefore only validates `{ access_token: string }`, the intended "any numeric property is the expiry" rule is never applied, and — because zod objects strip unknown keys — every other field of the sync-endpoint response (expiry/expiry_date, refresh_token, instance_url, api_domain, scope, token_type) is dropped from `data`. Downstream this corrupts stored credentials, e.g. zoomvideo sets `key.expiry_date = Math.round(Date.now() + newTokens.expires_in * 1000)` → `NaN`, office365 never updates its expiry, and salesforce persists a key without `instance_url`. Use `.passthrough()` plus an explicit expiry field, or validate per-app.

findings.title: Missing refresh_token is replaced with the literal string "refresh_token"
findings.body: When the parsed response has no `refresh_token`, the helper injects the literal string `"refresh_token"`. This value is then written to the DB by callers that merge the parse result into the stored key — e.g. `office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts` does `{...o365AuthCredentials, ...tokenResponse.data}` and `zoomvideo` does `key.refresh_token = newTokens.refresh_token`. Microsoft's refresh response legitimately may omit `refresh_token` (the schema marks it `optional()`), in which case the previously valid refresh token is destroyed and the credential can never be refreshed again — the user must re-install the app. The dummy value should never be persisted; preserve the existing refresh token instead.

findings.title: Sync path returns a raw fetch Response while several callers expect axios/googleapis shapes
findings.body: In the credential-sharing branch the helper returns the `Response` object from `fetch`. Callers do not all consume a `Response`: `googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts` reads `res?.data` (googleapis style), `zoho-bigin` and `zohocrm` read `tokenInfo.data.error` / `tokenInfo.data.access_token` (axios style), `hubspot` reads `hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn` (already-parsed object), and `larkcalendar` passes it to `handleLarkError` which expects the Lark `{code, data}` envelope. With syncing enabled these paths throw `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined` or silently compute `NaN` expiries, i.e. credential sync simply cannot work for those apps. The helper needs a single, documented return contract (e.g. always return parsed JSON) and the call sites must be adapted.

findings.title: Request to the credential sync endpoint is unauthenticated and its status is never checked
findings.body: The POST to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` carries only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` with no shared secret, signature, or auth header, so the self-hoster's token-vending endpoint cannot verify that the caller is Cal.com — anyone who can reach that URL can request a user's access token. The inbound direction (`/api/webhook/app-credential`) does require `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`; the outbound direction should be authenticated the same way. Additionally the response status is never checked (`response.ok`), so an error page/JSON from the endpoint flows into the token parsing and can be written to the credential.

findings.title: `prisma` is used but never imported in Salesforce CalendarService
findings.body: `await prisma.credential.update(...)` is added in `getClient()` but the file has no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"`. This is a type-check failure and, at runtime, a `ReferenceError: prisma is not defined` on every Salesforce calendar operation (the constructor calls `getClient`), breaking the Salesforce app entirely.

findings.title: Salesforce refreshes the token on every request but then connects with the old access token
findings.body: `getClient()` now unconditionally performs a `refresh_token` exchange on every instantiation of the service (no expiry check), yet the `jsforce.Connection` is still built with `credentialKey.access_token` / `credentialKey.instance_url` from the stale credential rather than the freshly obtained `accessTokenParsed.data`. The refresh therefore adds a blocking round trip (and Salesforce token-request rate-limit pressure) on every booking while not actually fixing an expired token. Use the newly returned `access_token`/`instance_url`, and only refresh when the stored token is expired.

findings.title: Zoho Bigin passes credentialId where refreshOAuthTokens expects userId
findings.body: `refreshOAuthTokens(fn, "zoho-bigin", credentialId)` — the third parameter of `refreshOAuthTokens` is `userId` and is sent to the sync endpoint as `calcomUserId`. Here the credential's primary key is passed instead of `credential.userId`, so with credential sharing enabled Cal.com asks the self-hosted endpoint for the tokens of a completely different (or non-existent) user, which at best fails and at worst installs another user's tokens on this credential. `refreshAccessToken` needs the userId plumbed through.

findings.title: Zoom sends appSlug "zoomvideo" which is not the app's slug
findings.body: `refreshOAuthTokens(..., "zoomvideo", credential.userId)` sends `appSlug=zoomvideo`, but the Zoom app's slug in the app store / `Credential.appId` is `zoom` (see `zoomvideo/api/callback.ts`, which creates the credential with `appId: "zoom"`), and the inbound webhook resolves apps by `prisma.app.slug`. The self-hoster therefore receives a slug that does not correspond to any Cal.com app id, so token sync for Zoom is keyed on the wrong identifier.

findings.title: Webex wires refreshOAuthTokens but still validates with the strict provider schema
findings.body: Webex now fetches tokens through `refreshOAuthTokens` (so a sync endpoint may answer with just an access token and expiry) yet still validates with `webexRefreshedTokenSchema.safeParse`, which requires an exact `scope` literal, `token_type: "Bearer"`, `refresh_token` and `refresh_token_expires_in`. Any sync response will fail parsing and reject with "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned", so Webex credential sharing cannot work. Either use `parseRefreshTokenResponse` here (as zoom/office365 do) or don't route Webex through the sync helper.

findings.title: Webhook handler has no method guard and throws unhandled errors on bad input
findings.body: `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` throws a `ZodError` for a malformed/absent body (e.g. any GET to this route), and `symmetricDecrypt` / `JSON.parse` throw for a wrong key or non-JSON plaintext. None of these are caught, so callers get a 500 with a Next.js error instead of a 4xx, and decryption stack traces end up in the logs. Add a `req.method !== "POST"` guard, use `safeParse`, and wrap the decrypt/parse in try/catch returning 400.

findings.title: Webhook secret compared with `!==` and header name not lowercased
findings.body: The shared secret is compared with a plain string comparison, which is not constant-time; use `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on equal-length buffers. Also, `req.headers` keys in Node are always lowercase, so if an operator sets `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME` with any uppercase character the lookup silently returns `undefined` and every request is rejected with "Invalid webhook secret" — apply `.toLowerCase()` to the configured header name rather than relying on the comment in `.env.example`.

findings.title: findFirst + create is ambiguous for multi-credential apps and racy
findings.body: Credentials are not unique per (userId, appId): a user can legitimately have several credentials for the same app (e.g. two Google Calendar accounts, and `larkcalendar`/`zoomvideo` callbacks explicitly deal with duplicates). `findFirst` picks an arbitrary one and overwrites its key, and the payload has no way to identify which credential to update. Two concurrent webhook deliveries will also both miss the `findFirst` and create duplicate credentials. Consider requiring a credential identifier in the payload and/or performing the read-modify-write in a transaction.

findings.title: APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED holds the encryption key value instead of a boolean
findings.body: `process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY` evaluates to the value of `CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY` (a secret) rather than `true`. The export is typed `string | undefined` and lives in a constants module that is imported broadly; any place that logs, serializes into props, or returns this constant would leak the AES key. Wrap it in `!!(...)` so only a boolean is ever exported.

findings.title: Token refresh failure detected via `response.statusText !== "OK"`
findings.body: Checking `statusText` is unreliable (it is empty for HTTP/2 responses and may differ per server), so a successful refresh can be rejected while the error message surfaced to the user is an empty string. Use `if (!response.ok)` and include the response body in the thrown error for diagnosability.

findings.title: No tests for the new OAuth sync helpers or webhook endpoint
findings.body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse`, `refreshOAuthTokens` and `/api/webhook/app-credential` are new shared primitives that touch every OAuth app's stored credentials, yet the PR adds no unit tests. The schema bug (computed `[z.string().toString()]` keys), the dummy `refresh_token` write, and the mismatched return shapes between call sites are exactly the kind of regressions a few table-driven tests on these two helpers (sharing enabled/disabled, response with and without refresh_token/expiry) plus a handler test for the webhook (bad secret, bad body, create vs update) would have caught.
